Formulation:
- Predisposing factors: history of thyroid disease (patient-reported) and high-demand occupation (law).
- Precipitating factors: recent job change with increased work stress; symptoms began around job change.
- Perpetuating factors: ongoing high occupational stress, possible biochemical thyrotoxicosis (overreplacement or uncontrolled disease) and/or episodic anxiety/panic maintaining sympathetic symptoms; ergonomic factors from prolonged computer/meeting work possibly contributing to headaches and hand paresthesias.
- Protective factors: patient is help-seeking, cooperative, denies substance misuse.
- Summary integration: The patient presents with episodic sympathetic symptoms (palpitations, heat intolerance, shortness of breath), frontal work-related headaches, bilateral hand paresthesias and reduced appetite/weight loss since a job change. DDx and the clinical picture raise primary concern for thyrotoxicosis (iatrogenic or uncontrolled) and a coexisting work-related anxiety/panic presentation; ergonomic/cervicogenic contributors and possible arrhythmia should be excluded.

Mental Health Care Plan Details

Principal Problem: Thyrotoxicosis (iatrogenic overreplacement or uncontrolled hyperthyroidism)
- Patient Goal(s):
  - Relief of palpitations, heat intolerance and return to baseline energy/weight/libido.
  - Clarify thyroid status and appropriate medication dosing.
- Clinical Goal(s):
  - Confirm thyroid function (TSH and free T4/T3), assess for biochemical thyrotoxicosis or overreplacement, perform focused cardiac and respiratory examination and ECG as indicated.
  - Adjust thyroxine therapy or refer to endocrinology if tests abnormal.
- Actions (Patient):
  - Attend in-person clinic appointment for examination and blood tests.
  - Bring current medication (thyroxine) and any records of prior thyroid tests if available.
- Actions (Clinician/GP):
  - Arrange in-person physical examination including heart rate, blood pressure, cardiovascular and respiratory exam.
  - Order thyroid function tests (TSH, free T4; consider free T3) and relevant baseline bloods as indicated.
  - Obtain ECG; consider ambulatory ECG monitoring if palpitations persist or arrhythmia suspected.
  - Review thyroxine dose and adherence; consider endocrinology referral if thyrotoxicosis confirmed or if dosing uncertain.
  - Do not initiate psychotropic medication for anxiety until reversible physical causes (thyroid / cardiac) are evaluated and managed.

Secondary Problem: Anxiety disorder / Panic attacks (work-related)
- Patient Goal(s):
  - Reduce frequency/severity of panic/anxiety symptoms, improve functioning at work, restore appetite and libido.
- Clinical Goal(s):
  - Provide psychoeducation, screen for anxiety/depression severity, initiate psychological interventions (brief CBT or workplace-focused therapy) as appropriate.
- Actions (Patient):
  - Practice short-term coping strategies (grounding/breathing techniques, brief breaks during meetings, reduce caffeine if applicable).
  - Accept referral for psychological therapy if offered; attend scheduled appointments.
- Actions (Clinician/GP):
  - Screen for anxiety and depression (e.g., GAD-7, PHQ-9) at in-person visit.
  - Provide psychoeducation that symptoms may be multifactorial (thyroid vs stress) and explain planned investigations.
  - Offer referral to psychological therapies (e.g., CBT) or occupational health for workplace adjustments.
  - Consider pharmacotherapy for anxiety only after medical causes are excluded/treated and after discussion with patient; document that clinician will not start psychotropic meds before in-person medical assessment (consistent with transcript).

Tertiary Problem: Work-related headaches / ergonomic strain and bilateral hand paresthesias
- Patient Goal(s):
  - Reduced headache frequency and hand tingling; improved comfort at work.
- Clinical Goal(s):
  - Assess for cervicogenic headache, carpal tunnel or radiculopathy; institute ergonomic measures and consider physiotherapy.
- Actions (Patient):
  - Implement ergonomic adjustments (chair/monitor/keyboard posture), take regular breaks, consider workplace assessment.
  - Record headache and paresthesia frequency/triggers for clinic review.
- Actions (Clinician/GP):
  - Perform musculoskeletal and neurological examination focusing on neck and upper limbs at in-person review.
  - If indicated, refer for physiotherapy/occupational therapy or nerve conduction studies/neurology if symptoms persistent or focal neurological signs present.

Patient Education, Emergency Care & Relapse Prevention:
- Education Given: Yes. Topics Covered:
  - Nature of symptoms, plan for in-person physical exam and thyroid tests; need to exclude medical causes before initiating psychiatric medication.
- Early Warning Signs of Relapse/Worsening:
  - New or worsening chest pain, syncope or presyncope, breathlessness at rest, sustained rapid heart rate, severe uncontrolled anxiety or emergence of suicidal thoughts.
- Coping Strategies:
  - Short breathing/grounding exercises during acute episodes, schedule brief breaks during meetings, reduce stimulants/caffeine, maintain medication adherence, seek workplace adjustments, engage with planned follow-up and investigations.

Summary of Differential Diagnoses (from DDx)
- Anxiety disorder / Panic attacks (High) — Symptoms are temporally/contextually related to work, with episodic palpitations, shortness of breath, paresthesias and high reported occupational stress; DDx ranks this high.
- Thyrotoxicosis (iatrogenic overreplacement or uncontrolled hyperthyroidism) (High) — Patient reports thyroid disease and thyroxine use plus classic sympathetic symptoms (palpitations, heat intolerance, weight loss, reduced libido); DDx ranks this high and recommends thyroid function testing.
- Tension-type / cervicogenic headache with ergonomic strain (Medium) — Headaches are frontal, work/computer related and began after job change; bilateral hand tingling may relate to repetitive posture or peripheral nerve irritation (DDx medium likelihood).

Quality checks
- Missing but clinically expected elements:
  - No vital signs, ECG or physical examination findings documented.
  - No laboratory results (thyroid function tests) available.
  - Formal screening scores for anxiety/depression (e.g., GAD-7/PHQ-9) not recorded.
  - No documented follow-up/review date.
- Internal conflicts between transcript and DDx:
  - Conflict noted: patient reports "hyperthyroidism" and also reports taking thyroxine — DDx highlights possible inconsistency (thyroxine usually replacement for hypothyroidism; could reflect iatrogenic overreplacement, prior treatment history, or patient misreporting).
- Transcript quality notes:
  - Several short pauses, occasional overlapping/hesitant speech by patient; dialogue captures core symptoms and context but lacks formal MSE, vitals, or objective exam data.
